title: Reading practice: A Letter and Two Library Systems
description: A student’s persuasive letter and a comparison of two class book systems: reasons and evidence, word meaning, comparing, and following a routine.

stimuli.title: A Letter to Our Principal
paragraphs: I am writing to ask you to let each class read outside for twenty minutes every Friday. I am a student in Room 11, and I believe outdoor reading would make our school better.

First, fresh air helps students feel awake and calm. Last month, our class sat under a tree for a drawing lesson, and nobody was sleepy. Second, reading outside gives students more room. Some of us like the grass, and others like a bench, so everyone can find a comfortable spot. Third, students will read more if they enjoy the place. In a survey, our teacher asked every student in our class whether they would read more outside. Eighteen of 24 said yes.

Some teachers worry that students will be distracted outside. They think students will watch birds and clouds instead of reading. I understand this worry. However, we could make rules. For example, each student could pick a quiet spot, and the teacher could stay in the shade nearby.
For these reasons, I hope you will say yes to Friday outdoor reading. Thank you for thinking about my idea.

stimuli.title: Two Ways to Borrow Class Books
paragraphs: Room 12 and Room 14 both have a class library. Each room has a shelf near the door, and students may keep a borrowed book for one week. The two rooms keep track of the books in different ways.

In Room 12, students use a sign-out sheet. A student writes the book title, her name, and the date on the sheet. When she returns the book, she crosses out the line. The sheet hangs on the wall, so the teacher can see all the borrowed books on one page. However, students sometimes forget to cross out a line, and then the sheet is not correct.

In Room 14, students use name cards. Each student has a card with his or her name. To borrow a book, a student takes the book from the shelf and puts the name card in the empty space where the book was. When the student returns the book, he or she takes the card back and puts the book in the same space. Because the card sits where the book was, everyone can see who has each book. Still, a student who loses a card cannot borrow a book until the teacher makes a new one.

Last week, the teachers asked all the classes to use the same system in every class library. Two students in Room 12 gave their opinions. Lena said, “I think we should use cards. We do not need to write anything.” Marcus said, “I disagree. The teacher can see all the books on one page with the sheet.”

items.stem: Which sentence is the claim in Priya’s letter?

options.text: Fresh air helps students feel awake and calm when they read.
Some teachers worry that students will be distracted outside.
Eighteen of 24 students said they would read more outside.
Each class should read outside for twenty minutes every Friday.

distractors.a: This sentence is a reason Priya gives. It tells why outdoor reading would help, not what she wants.
distractors.b: This is a worry that some teachers have. Priya answers it, but it is not her claim.
distractors.c: This is evidence from a survey. It supports the claim, but it is not the claim.

items.explanation: The claim is what Priya wants the principal to do: let each class read outside for twenty minutes every Friday. Fresh air is a reason, the survey result is evidence, and the distraction worry belongs to some teachers.

support.clue: A claim is the main thing a writer wants. Reread the first paragraph of the letter, then ask which choice is a reason, which is evidence, and which is someone else’s worry.
support.frame: Priya’s claim is what she wants the principal to ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different letter). A writer asks for a second water fountain near the gym. “Students get thirsty after games” is a reason. “Last week, 12 of 15 students said they were thirsty” is evidence. “The school should add a second fountain” is the claim.

Now find the claim in Priya’s letter.

misconceptions.a: mistakes a reason for the claim
misconceptions.b: mistakes a worry for the claim

items.stem: Sort each sentence from the letter: is it a reason, or is it evidence (an example or a number)?

tokens.text: Fresh air helps students feel awake and calm.
Eighteen of 24 students in Room 11 said they would read more outside.
Reading outside gives students more room.
During the drawing lesson under the tree, nobody was sleepy.

zones.label: Evidence: an example or a number

items.explanation: Fresh air and more room are reasons. The survey result and the drawing lesson are things that happened or numbers that can be checked, so they are evidence.

support.clue: A reason tells why an idea is good. Evidence shows a real example or a number. Look for numbers and for events that happened.
support.frame: The reason is ______, and the evidence is ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different letter). Reason: “A school garden helps students learn.” Evidence: “After the garden project, 20 of 25 students could name three plant parts.” The reason tells why. The evidence is a number that supports it.

Now sort the sentences from Priya’s letter into reasons and evidence.

items.stem: Which two sentences show how Priya answers people who disagree with her idea?

options.text: Priya thanks the principal for thinking about her idea.
Priya says that she understands the teachers’ worry.
Priya tells the principal that she is a student in Room 11.
Priya suggests that each student could pick a quiet spot.

distractors.a: This is a polite closing. It does not respond to the worry about distraction.
distractors.c: This tells who the writer is. It does not respond to the worry.

items.explanation: Priya shows she understands the worry and then offers a rule that could solve the problem.

support.clue: Find the paragraph that begins “Some teachers worry.” Look for the sentences that answer that worry.
support.frame: Priya answers the worry by ______ and by ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different letter). A student asks for a longer recess. A teacher worries about noise. The student writes, “That is a fair concern,” and offers to keep the games on the far field.

Now find the two sentences where Priya answers the worry.

misconceptions.c: uses an introduction as a reply

items.stem: Match each word from the letter with its meaning in the letter.

right.text: a list of rules that students must follow at school
a feeling that something bad may happen
a set of questions that finds out what many people think
not able to keep your attention on one thing

items.explanation: The sentences around each word explain it: the teacher asked every student a question, students might watch birds instead of reading, and teachers think something may go wrong.

support.clue: Read the sentences before and after each word, and ask what the writer is describing there.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different word). “The class was thrilled. Everyone cheered and jumped up.” The words after “thrilled” show it means very excited. Look at what people do near a word to find its meaning.

Now use the sentences around each word in the letter to find its meaning.

items.stem: Sort each detail: does it describe Room 12 only, Room 14 only, or both rooms?

tokens.text: Students write the book title on a sheet.
Students put a name card in the empty space on the shelf.
Students may keep a book for one week.
The class library shelf is near the door.
A lost card means no borrowing until a new one is made.

items.explanation: The sign-out sheet belongs to Room 12, and the name cards belong to Room 14. The one-week limit and the shelf near the door are the same in both rooms.

support.clue: The first paragraph tells what is the same in both rooms. The next two paragraphs each describe one room.
support.frame: ______ is true for Room 12, ______ is true for Room 14, and ______ is true for both.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different comparison). Two bakeries are on one street. Both open at 7:00. One sells only bread, and the other sells only cakes. “Open at 7:00” is true for both. “Only bread” is true for one bakery. “Only cakes” is true for the other.

Now sort each detail about the two class libraries in the same way.

items.stem: Choose the best connecting word for each blank to compare the two rooms.

dropdown.template: Room 12 uses a sign-out sheet, {1} Room 14 uses name cards. In {2} rooms, students may keep a book for one week. A sheet shows every borrowed book in one place. {3}, students sometimes forget to cross out a line.

items.explanation: “While” shows a difference between the two rooms. “Both of the” shows something the same. “However” shows a problem that goes against the good point just stated.

support.clue: Ask whether each blank joins ideas that are different, the same, or in conflict. The first paragraph and the second paragraph show you.
support.frame: Room 12 does ______, while Room 14 does ______. Both rooms ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different comparison). “A pencil can be erased, while a pen cannot. Both are used for writing.” The word “while” shows a difference, and “both” shows a way they are the same.

Now choose words that show differences and sameness between the two rooms.

items.stem: In Room 14, how does a student borrow and return a book? Put the steps in order.

items.text: Take your name card back and put the book in the same space.
Before you walk away, put your name card in the empty space where the book was.
Take a book from the shelf.
Read the book during the week you have it.

items.explanation: A student takes the book and puts the name card in its space before leaving the shelf, reads the book during the week, and then swaps the card for the book when returning it.

support.clue: Read the paragraph about Room 14. Ask what must happen before the card can go in the empty space, and what must happen before the card comes back.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different routine). To use a classroom marker box: First, take a marker from the box. Next, put a colored clip on the box edge. After that, use the marker. Last, put the marker back and take your clip.

Now put the steps of the Room 14 routine in order in the same way.

items.stem: Lena and Marcus each choose a system. Which two details are reasons they give?

options.text: Marcus says “I disagree” to show that he has a different opinion.
Lena says that cards mean students do not need to write anything.
Marcus says the teacher can see all the books on one page with the sheet.
The passage says that Room 12 and Room 14 both have a class library.

distractors.a: “I disagree” tells that Marcus has a different opinion, but it does not give a reason.
distractors.d: This is background about the two rooms. It is not something Lena or Marcus says to support a choice.

items.explanation: Lena’s reason for cards is that nothing needs to be written. Marcus’s reason for the sheet is that the teacher can see all the books on one page.

support.clue: Look at the last paragraph. A reason tells why a system is good. A sentence that only shows disagreement does not tell why.
support.frame: Lena’s reason is that ______, and Marcus’s reason is that ______.
support.model:
Mentor example (a different talk). One student says, “We should eat outside. It is sunny.” Another says, “I disagree. The tables inside are cleaner.” “It is sunny” is a reason. “I disagree” is not a reason. “The tables inside are cleaner” is a reason.

Now find the two reasons in Lena and Marcus’s talk.

misconceptions.a: mistakes an opinion for a reason
